title: From AI ambition to business impact
body: From AI ambition to business impact Nov 12, 2026 | Rodrigo Kede Lima - President, Microsoft Frontier Company Most business leaders I meet no longer need to be convinced that AI works. They’ve seen the pilots, the demos and the copilots. The question I hear in boardrooms now is different: How do we move from AI that impresses to AI that changes how the business actually runs? That is the question Microsoft Frontier Company was built to answer, and to date, we have engaged on nearly 500 projects with over 200 customers across 28 countries. Customers including 3M, Alaska Airlines, BMW, Core42, KT, Land O’Lakes, London Stock Exchange Group, Mastercard, McKesson, Northern Trust, Novo Nordisk, Publicis Groupe, Saint-Gobain, Siemens and Unilever are seeing real value from working side by side with our Forward Deployed Engineering teams. More importantly, most customers where we have completed initial projects have returned for additional engagements, generating hundreds of follow-on projects. Customers don’t come back for engineers. They come back because the first engagement delivered something they could measure and they can see the next workflow worth redesigning. The technology is ready. What slows AI down is everything around it. That means identifying where AI can deliver the greatest value, building in trust and governance, redesigning the operating models and helping people work in new ways. Technology and people have to move forward together. What this looks like in practice Unilever is collaborating with Microsoft engineers to bring AI into its factories. On the factory floor, intelligent technology helps teams boost efficiency and deliver superior products to customers. In Pondicherry factory — Unilever’s largest Home Care Liquids factory in South Asia and a 2026 World Economic Forum Lighthouse site — a digital twin built on NVIDIA Omniverse and hosted on Azure simulates a real factory environment with integrated live data. This helps anticipate issues before they occur, monitors performance in real time and guides operators through the fixes and recommendations. 3M is working with our engineers to help its Global Business Services team automate customer order management. The companies are building an AI agent-driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. The solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve speed and consistency and accelerate cash flow — freeing staff for higher-value work while enabling scalable, auditable operations. Publicis Groupe is co-building with our engineers to bring AI into the heart of how it works and delivers for clients. Microsoft engineers work side by side with Publicis teams to design and build agentic processes grounded in Microsoft IQ, so agents work with the business context, data and knowledge behind Publicis’ work. These processes use reinforcement learning, drawing on real-world outcomes and human feedback to keep improving how the agents perform over time. The approach combines very fast engineering with hands-on knowledge transfer, helping Publicis build lasting AI capability. The work builds on Publicis’ rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to all 114,000 of its employees. Northern Trust needed to accelerate onboarding to its Asset Servicing Front Office Solutions platform, a process that took about two and a half weeks per client. Our engineers worked alongside Northern Trust’s experts to build an AI-powered onboarding agent within the Excel and SharePoint tools analysts already use. The result: data preparation time fell 83%, from two and a half weeks to three days, with 96.5% first pass quality score in testing . Analysts remain in control while gaining more time for higher-value client service. KT , one of South Korea’s largest telecommunications providers, wanted to help network operators identify and respond to problems faster. Our engineers worked from KT’s offices to co-build AIO-Net, a continuously learning AI agent platform informed by KT’s operating procedures and veteran network experts. It now detects network issues in two to three minutes, down from more than ten, while keeping people in control of decisions and actions. Saint-Gobain , the 360-year-old construction materials company, is using AI to help reduce the carbon footprint of cement. Working alongside its researchers, Microsoft engineers used Microsoft Discovery to gather 62,000 patents and 44,000 research abstracts into a knowledge base in hours, work Saint-Gobain estimates would have taken researchers a year. In about six weeks, the team identified new hypotheses for cement additives that scientists are now testing in the lab. Across all of these customers, the pattern is the same: Begin with the value , not the technology. Redesign the process , not just the task. Build in fast cycles with the customer’s teams. Put security, governance and cost management in place from day one , so scaling doesn’t stall. This is how organizations move from isolated AI projects to sustainable transformation: by focusing on measurable outcomes, redesigning work and building the capabilities to keep improving over time. New research from IDC underscores why this approach matters. While 66% of organizations report substantial or transformative results from AI, only 48% are scaling or seeing consistent value across their organizations. At the same time, 71% expect AI spending to increase by at least 10% in the next year, putting even greater pressure on businesses to demonstrate measurable returns. The challenge is no longer simply adopting AI. It is reimagining how work gets done and turning that transformation into lasting business impact. We’re holding ourselves to the same standard If we’re asking customers to redesign how they work around AI, we have to do the same. Microsoft Frontier Company was deliberately designed to be flat and fast, with one front door for customers, and as a reference for what an AI-native organization can look like. We are learning, adjusting and moving fast, the same way we ask our customers to. The real measure of success The gap between AI that impresses and AI that delivers won’t close on its own. It closes workflow by workflow, with people who understand the business sitting next to people who can build. Our success will be measured by more than what we deliver. The real test is what our customers can do after we’ve worked together: run, govern and improve their own AI systems, on their terms, with their intelligence protected. Their success is the clearest measure of ours. Learn more at www.microsoft.com/en-us/frontier-company . Rodrigo Kede Lima is the President of Microsoft Frontier Company and leads the operating business of 6,000 industry and engineering experts focused on delivering Frontier Transformation through AI for customers around the world. NOTE IDC Infographic, sponsored by Microsoft, The Real Business Value of AI, IDC #US54985026-IG, November 2026 Tags: AI , Azure , Microsoft 365 Copilot , Microsoft Frontier Company

title: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms
body: Scaling AI value without losing control: Lessons from Frontier Firms Nov 12, 2026 | Alysa Taylor - Chief Marketing Officer, Commercial Cloud & AI Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC , commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain. In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale. What the research found Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters. Measurement is the next test . Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy. “Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC. AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses. Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability. Where scale stalls 66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them. The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design. Inside the Frontier Firm IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause. What they do differently comes down to five behaviors: They invest ahead of plan . 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend. They deploy AI broadly , across most of the business, not just a few teams. They put agents to work . 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows. They govern so they can scale . 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters. They build skills everywhere . 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters. At Bristol Myers Squibb , the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time. Four disciplines for scaling AI value The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off. I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER . “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.” Unlock model choice Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data. Redesign workflows around agents Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters. Govern decisions and actions Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do. Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.” Measure and optimize value Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest. Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start. Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch. Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall. What this means for business The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation. First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day. Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business. Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI. The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next. Get the full picture Download the global infographic , The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe , Asia Pacific and the Americas . The full InfoBrief will follow. Alysa Taylor is the Chief Marketing Officer for Commercial Cloud and AI at Microsoft, leading teams that enable digital and AI transformation for organizations of all sizes across the globe. retained_feed_body: Results are widespread. Value at scale is not, and that gap is what this year’s research from IDC , commissioned by Microsoft, set out to explain. In our fourth year commissioning IDC, more than 5,200 senior IT and business leaders across 28 industries shared what it takes to maximize value as AI scales. The clearest lessons come from Frontier Firms, the group last year’s research introduced: the top 10% of organizations on IDC’s AI maturity scale. What the research found Frontier Firms lead on return. They report an average 4x return on AI versus 2.7x for slow adopters (the bottom 30% on IDC’s scale), and 39% see returns of 5x or more versus 4% of slow adopters. Measurement is the next test . Only 61% of organizations are highly confident they can measure AI’s business value and ROI, versus 93% of Frontier Firms. Governance is in place, but confidence lags. 65% of organizations have an established process to govern agents, yet only 60% have high confidence in addressing AI security and governance risks. Workforce readiness is uneven. 67% say their workforce reports high trust in AI, yet only 20% have a comprehensive, organization-wide skilling strategy. “Organizations that scale AI value aren’t simply spending more. They manage AI investments, models, agents, governance and skills as one discipline, and that is what turns early results into value they can repeat across the business,” says Kathy Lange, Research Director, AI, Data and Automation Software, IDC. AI value now reaches well beyond cost savings Organizations now use AI in 6.5 business areas on average, led by IT infrastructure, cybersecurity and customer service, with the fastest growth in industry-specific uses. Employee experience, revenue growth, customer experience, innovation and risk reduction now rank nearly even as the places AI strengthens the business. Cost is an important consideration, but it is evaluated alongside accuracy, security, compliance and scalability. Where scale stalls 66% of leaders say AI has delivered substantial or transformative results, but only 48% are scaling that value across multiple business units. Agents follow the same pattern: 36% of organizations are still piloting them. The widest gap is people: workforce confidence is running well ahead of the plans to support it. The organizations pulling ahead are closing these gaps by design. Inside the Frontier Firm IDC’s maturity scale weighs spending discipline, breadth of use, agent adoption, skills, confidence in managing AI risk and outcomes. On agents specifically, Frontier Firms report a 3.8x return versus 3.0x for slow adopters. These returns are leader-reported, and the research shows association rather than cause. What they do differently comes down to five behaviors: They invest ahead of plan . 90% of Frontier Firms exceeded their planned AI spend. They deploy AI broadly , across most of the business, not just a few teams. They put agents to work . 96% are rolling out agents at scale, and 53% orchestrate them across workflows. They govern so they can scale . 87% have a process to govern and oversee agents, versus 51% of slow adopters. They build skills everywhere . 80% have an organization-wide AI skilling strategy, versus 3% of slow adopters. At Bristol Myers Squibb , the RABIT agent “connects the dots across meetings, helping teams make better decisions while reducing administrative follow-up work,” says Lakshman Yerramalla, Director of Portfolio Governance and Delivery for Global Manufacturing Operations. Project managers who use it save up to an estimated 20% of their time. Four disciplines for scaling AI value The lesson from Frontier Firms is one I believe every leader can act on: scaling AI value means managing models, agents, governance and measurement as one accountable system. Value and control aren’t a trade-off. I see the same pattern with customers: the organizations scaling fastest treat AI as a change in how the business runs, not a technology rollout. “The skilling that a lot of companies miss is the business skilling,” says Eric Tabor, Chief Digital Officer, KOHLER . “We also focus on how to dissect processes and convert them into AI workflows.” Unlock model choice Trust and security, leading-edge technology and model performance tie as the top criteria for choosing an AI platform (44% each). Match the right model to each job, balancing cost with protection of intellectual property and data. Redesign workflows around agents Agents create the most value when work is redesigned around them. The bigger opportunity is what they free people to do more of: leaders point to creativity, innovation and business reinvention (41%), customer-facing work and relationships (39%) and analytical work and data interpretation (39%). Connect agents across processes, with human oversight where it matters. Govern decisions and actions Trust is building faster than confidence. Most leaders report high trust in their AI systems, yet fewer are highly confident addressing security and governance risks. As agents take on more of the work, trust has to be earned continuously, and governance has to reach beyond models to keep people in control of what agents decide and do. Conagra Brands made governance its starting point. “Laying the foundation of proper governance, observability and responsible AI was our first step to engaging our employees with AI,” says Tracy Schaefer, Chief Information Officer, Conagra Brands. “We built a SteerCo to review risk factors, access and identity management.” Measure and optimize value Connect investment and performance data to business outcomes, compare how processes perform before and after AI and direct spending where it delivers the most value. With 71% of organizations expecting AI budgets to rise 10% or more in the next 12 months, this discipline will separate leaders from the rest. Underneath all four disciplines are people. None of it scales without an organization-wide plan to build AI skills. That’s where Frontier Firms are furthest ahead, and it’s where I’d urge every leader to start. Black & Veatch reached 98% adoption of Microsoft 365 Copilot through deliberate change management, including early-adopter cohorts that surfaced real business use cases. “Our goal is to be a Frontier Firm. The intention is not to stop at pure adoption,” says Mike Adams, Chief Digital Technology Officer, Black & Veatch. Go deeper at Microsoft Ignite IDC Executive Analyst Shari Lava will lead three sessions at Microsoft Ignite on Nov. 18, including The AI ROI Divide: Why Some Organizations Scale and Others Stall. What this means for business The gap that matters now isn’t between companies that use AI and those that don’t. It’s between those getting results in pockets and those turning AI into repeatable value across the business. There are three key ways leaders can step into this kind of transformation. First, treat AI as business transformation, not a technology rollout. Frontier Firms connect AI to the outcomes that matter most, from growth to customer experience, and manage it as one accountable system. That is the heart of Frontier Transformation, and it’s the work we’re doing alongside our customers every day. Second, start with your own function. In marketing, we’re applying these same disciplines to our own work: redesigning workflows around agents, setting clear guardrails and measuring what AI actually delivers. Every function can become its own proof point for the rest of the business. Third, invest in people as much as in technology. Skills are the widest gap in this year’s research, and it’s the one I care about most. The organizations that pull ahead will be the ones where everyone, at every level, has the support to learn, experiment and grow with AI. The next phase of AI won’t be defined by who uses it. It will be defined by who can scale its value and stay in control. This research gives every leader a benchmark for where they stand today and a clear view of what to do next. Get the full picture Download the global infographic , The Real Business Value of AI, to see a summary of findings and benchmark your organization against Frontier Firms before your next AI investment review. Regional infographics are also available for Europe , Asia Pacific and the Americas . The full InfoBrief will follow. body: A New Dawn in the Cloud: ‘Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV’ Is Coming to GeForce NOW Plus, catch NVIDIA DLSS 5 updates for ‘War Thunder’ and ‘Where Winds Meet,’ and dive into ‘Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen,’ alongside 10 new games. November 12, 2026 by GeForce NOW Community 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Rally the ranks this GFN Thursday. Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV is coming to GeForce NOW , allowing players to experience the battle for Kronus through cloud gaming. There’s more on the horizon, with NVIDIA DLSS 5 technology coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet . Meanwhile, Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen brings new tales and encounters, alongside 10 games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Kronus Calls for Reinforcements Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War IV , developed by KING Art Games and published by Deep Silver, is coming to GeForce NOW. Launching on Steam Thursday, Dec. 3, the real-time strategy game returns to the series’ roots with large-scale battles, base building and a renewed fight for planet Kronus. Command the Space Marines, Orks, Necrons or the Adeptus Mechanicus, which makes their series debut. Build a base, secure resources and customize squads to the conflict across more than 70 campaign missions, playable solo or in co-op mode. The Last Stand, Skirmish and multiplayer modes offer more ways to put tactics to the test. GeForce NOW will bring the action to supported PCs, Macs, handhelds and other devices, with game downloads and updates handled in the cloud. Save the storage space for everyday essentials and planning for the next offensive. Wishlist the game on Steam , and stay tuned to GFN Thursday to prepare for launch. DLSS 5 Keeps on Coming NVIDIA DLSS 5 continues to evolve, with Gaijin Entertainment’s War Thunder and Everstone Studio’s Where Winds Meet next to receive support for the technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature. Arriving in mid-November, War Thunder ’s Eagle’s Shadow major update adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, dozens of new planes, ships and tanks, along with cluster bombs for planes and visual-effects enhancements increasing the realism and dynamism of battle. In Where Winds Meet , DLSS support arrives Monday, Nov. 23, enhancing the environments and characters of its wuxia open-world action role-playing game. Both titles will use the latest DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering model, released in October, which doubles model performance compared with the previous version. Since its initial announcement in March, model performance has improved tenfold, bringing the technology to more gamers, including GeForce NOW Ultimate members streaming with GeForce RTX 5080 cloud rigs. Get a closer look at the DLSS updates and find more details . A New Tale for the Arisen Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen is streaming on GeForce NOW, expanding the deep, explorable fantasy world of Dragon’s Dogma 2 with new tales and encounters. Travel to the long-abandoned region of Norgan, join the enigmatic Eir and uncover the secrets of the undying Fallen Dragon. Unearth forgotten relics to unlock powerful weapons and skills, take on Lost Rites’ 12 dungeon challenges and explore new hairstyles and tattoos for Arisen and Pawn customization. Delicious in Dungeon also arrives in the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with a special collaboration. GeForce NOW keeps all the new downloadable content available across supported devices — without a single download claiming local storage on a gamer’s hardware of choice. In addition, members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week: Worst Class Ever (New release on Steam , Nov. 9) Ashes of the Singularity II (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Cyberpunk 2077 ( Xbox Play Anywhere, new release on Battle.net , Nov. 10) DreamWorks Shrek 2 Remastered (New release on Steam , Nov. 10) Warhammer Survivors (New release on Steam and Xbox , available on Game Pass, Nov. 10) Main Sequence (New release on Steam , Nov. 12) Deadly Days: Roadtrip ( Steam ) GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend ( Steam , Ultimate members) Graveyard Keeper ( Steam ) Tape to Tape ( Steam ) Also this week, Ultimate members can take a trip back to 2006 with GeForce 8800 GTX – 20 Years of a Legend , a playable demo celebrating the iconic GPU’s 20th anniversary with DLSS 4.5 and path tracing in the cloud. Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles. Those ready to put the next game plan into action can grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate, with the cost applicable toward a first monthly membership. title: Navarre Woman Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Drug Trafficking
body: Press Release Navarre Woman Sentenced to Five Years in Federal Prison for Drug Trafficking Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Pensacola, Florida – Loredana Alessandra Bassolino, 38, of Navarre, Florida was sentenced to five years in federal prison after previously pleading guilty to possession with intent to distribute more than 40 grams of fentanyl and more than 5 grams of methamphetamine. The sentence was announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “Thanks to the excellent investigative work of the DEA, with support from the Gulf Coast HIDTA and our U.S. Marshals, and this successful prosecution by my office, this drug trafficker will be kept off our streets. President Donald J. Trump and Attorney General Todd Blanche remain fully committed to delivering the safe, drug-free communities that our citizens deserve, and my office will fulfill that promise with aggressive prosecutions like this one to hold the peddlers of deadly drugs accountable.” Court documents reflect that on January 14, 2026, federal agents executed an arrest warrant for Andre Perry at a hotel in Pensacola, Florida. When law enforcement made entry into Perry’s hotel room to effectuate the arrest, they observed drug paraphernalia littered throughout the room, along with a “speed loader” tool used to quickly load ammunition into firearm magazines. Bassolino, another occupant of the hotel room, admitted that narcotics were present and gave consent to search the room. During their search, law enforcement discovered fentanyl, methamphetamine, and a loaded firearm. Both Bassolino and Perry are convicted felons who are legally prohibited from possessing firearms or ammunition, with Perry most recently being convicted of possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine and fentanyl and possession with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine and fentanyl in July 2025. “Fentanyl remains the biggest drug threat facing our country,” said Special Agent in Charge Daniel Escobar, DEA Tampa Field Division. “Our agents and law enforcement partners remain vigilant in the fight to rid our communities of traffickers who distribute this poison to our citizens.” Perry is scheduled for sentencing on February 11, 2027, at 2:00 pm before United States District Judge T. Kent Wetherell, II in Pensacola, Florida. The conviction and sentence were the result of an investigation by the Drug Enforcement Administration with assistance from the United States Marshals Service and the Gulf Coast High Intensity Drug Trafficking Areas (HIDTA) Task Force. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Thomas S.P. Geeker. Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN) is the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities. title: Two Co-Defendants Sentenced to a Total of Nearly 13 Years for Unlawful Possession of a Firearm and Ammunition
body: Press Release Two Co-Defendants Sentenced to a Total of Nearly 13 Years for Unlawful Possession of a Firearm and Ammunition Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of Florida Gainesville, Florida – Kelvin Quentin Scott Wright, 32, of Gainesville, Florida, was sentenced to four years and nine months of federal imprisonment, and Reginald Duante Davis, 36, of Gainesville, Florida, was sentenced to eight years of federal imprisonment for possession of a firearm and ammunition by a convicted felon. The sentences were announced by John P. Heekin, United States Attorney for the Northern District of Florida. U.S. Attorney Heekin said: “This successful prosecution ensures these dangerous, armed criminals will be kept off our streets for several years. Our state and federal law enforcement partners are committed to keeping our communities safe, and my office will continue to back up their efforts with aggressive prosecutions of dangerous criminals to ensure our citizens get the crime-free streets and neighborhoods they deserve.” Court records reflect that on April 12, 2024, Alachua County Sheriff’s Office stopped a vehicle for multiple traffic violations. The driver was Kelvin Wright and his co-defendant Reginald Davis was the front seat passenger. Both defendants are prohibited from possessing a firearm or ammunition as convicted felons. During the probable cause search of the vehicle, a loaded firearm, marijuana, oxycodone, and nearly 28 grams of crack cocaine were located in the center console. The DNA of both defendants was located on the firearm in various locations. “Keeping firearms out of the hands of convicted felons is critical to protecting our communities from more violence,” said FBI Jacksonville Special Agent in Charge Jason Carley. “The FBI will always work closely with our partners to identify repeat offenders and hold them accountable for their actions.  This case highlights the importance of how strong partnerships make a real difference in keeping our communities safe.” “The federal sentencing in this case underscores our commitment to keeping guns out of the hands of convicted felons,” said Alachua County Sheriff Chad D. Scott. “I am grateful for the strong partnership between our deputies, federal agencies, and prosecutors who work together every day to protect the safety of Alachua County.” The case was jointly investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the Alachua County Sheriff’s Office. The case was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Christie S. Utt. title: Jefferson County Man Sentenced to Over 21 Years in Prison for Receipt and  Possession of Child Pornography
body: Press Release Jefferson County Man Sentenced to Over 21 Years in Prison for Receipt and  Possession of Child Pornography Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov James Yerdon, age 56, of Adams Center, New York, was sentenced Monday, November 9, 2026, in federal court to 262 months in federal prison for receiving and possessing child pornography. First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III, Anthony Patrone, Acting Special Agent in Charge of the Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and New York State Police (NYSP) Superintendent Steven G. James made the announcement. As part of his prior guilty plea, Yerdon, a previously convicted sex offender, admitted that on May 13, 2025, he possessed multiple images and videos of child pornography that he had downloaded from the internet including material depicting the sexual abuse of children as young as five months old. The defendant also possessed nude images of a 7-year-old child Yerdon had created during a trip Yerdon took with the child to the Albany, New York area. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sarcone stated: “The defendant’s conduct in this case is horrific and is deserving of the lengthy sentence imposed today. The defendant is a repeat offender who not only sought out and accumulated child pornography online, but he also directly targeted children in our community. I am grateful to HSI and the New York State Police for their tireless work protecting our communities and especially our children from predators like the defendant.” NYSP Superintendent Steven G. James said, “Mr. Yerdon had no regard for his victims or their well-being, instead he took advantage of them in the most deplorable manner. This case serves as a reminder that those who prey on vulnerable and defenseless individuals, especially when they are in a place of trust, will be fully prosecuted. The State Police is committed to our partnership with the United States Attorney’s Office and Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations to intercept these predators and bring an end to the damage they inflict.” In addition to the term of imprisonment, Chief U.S. District Judge, Brenda K. Sannes, also sentenced Yerdon to serve a 20-year term of supervised release, to begin after Yerdon is released from prison, at which time Yerdon will also be required to register as a sex offender. Yerdon was also ordered to pay $26,000 in restitution to victims of his offense. The case was investigated by HSI and NYSP and was prosecuted by Assistant United States Attorney Adrian LaRochelle as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New York, Northern

title: New York Doctor Charged in $6.8M Medicare Fraud Scheme
body: Press Release New York Doctor Charged in $6.8M Medicare Fraud Scheme Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs A federal grand jury in the Southern District of Florida returned an indictment on Tuesday charging Dr. Edgard Salazar, 57, of Armonk, New York, with conspiring to bill Medicare for thousands of consultations that never occurred and millions of dollars of orthotic braces that Medicare patients did not want or need. According to court documents, telemedicine company TelevisitMD allegedly allowed Salazar to sign pre-filled prescriptions for Medicare beneficiaries who did not need the orthotic braces ordered in the prescriptions. Salazar did not examine or treat the beneficiaries and often did not speak to them at all. At times, when Salazar did speak to the beneficiaries, they told Salazar they did not want or need orthotic braces. Salazar signed prescriptions for them anyway. Salazar also billed Medicare for telemedicine consultations that he never performed. Salazar allegedly participated in submitting over $6.8 million in false and fraudulent claims to Medicare. Christopher Harwood owned and operated TelevisitMD. In March 2026, Harwood pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud and agreed to pay $17.9 million in restitution. Last month, Harwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in the conspiracy. Salazar is charged with conspiracy to commit health care fraud and five counts of health care fraud. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison on each count. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division; Special Agent in Charge Brett Skiles of the FBI Miami Field Office; and Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) made the announcement. FBI and HHS-OIG investigated the case. Trial Attorney Owen Dunn of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section is prosecuting the case. On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs. The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at https://www.justice.gov/fraud/health-care-fraud-section . An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. Updated November 12, 2026 Topic Fraud Component National Fraud Enforcement Division Press Release Number: 26-1352

title: Big Stone Gap Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Possession of a Firearm
body: Press Release Big Stone Gap Man Pleads Guilty to Illegal Possession of a Firearm Thursday, November 12, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Western District of Virginia ABINGDON, Va. – A Big Stone Gap man, with a history of drug distribution, pled guilty last week to illegally possessing a firearm as a previously convicted felon. Jeremy Michael Boggs, 45, pled guilty last week to one count of possessing a firearm after having been convicted of a felony. Boggs has agreed to be sentenced to a term of imprisonment between eight and twelve years. According to court documents, on January 7, 2026, law enforcement received a call for trespassing at an apartment building in Wise, Virginia. Upon arriving at the scene, officers located Boggs in the laundry room of the apartment building and learned Boggs had an outstanding warrant for his arrest. As officers searched Boggs pursuant to his arrest on the outstanding warrant, an officer located an empty holster on Boggs’s belt. Wrapped inside a jacket Boggs had been wearing, officers found a loaded, Smith and Wesson revolver. In one of the jacket pockets, officers found a bag containing nine additional rounds of ammunition. Boggs was prohibited from possessing firearms due to at least four previous felony convictions in Virginia and Tennessee, including for drug distribution and aggravated assault. First Assistant United States Attorney Robert N. Tracci and Anthony Spotswood, Special Agent in Charge, ATF Washington Division, made the announcement made the announcement. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, Wise Police Department, and Wise County Sheriff’s Office investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Corey Hall is prosecuting the case. title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
body:
Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) , the AWS SDKs , and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub . You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker. How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ . You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged. From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region. The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS. If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally. Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023 . The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/ , so it’s on the path. PKG=https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest
sudo dnf install -y $PKG/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

aws-emulator -v On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image. I started the emulator with aws-emulator . It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 , so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file. aws-emulator In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials. export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1
unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR , so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000 . curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

aws sts get-caller-identity Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it. $ aws s3 mb s3://local-getting-started
make_bucket: local-getting-started

$ echo "hello from the emulator" > hello.txt

$ aws s3 cp hello.txt s3://local-getting-started/
upload: ./hello.txt to s3://local-getting-started/hello.txt

$ aws s3 ls s3://local-getting-started/ With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them. Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account. kiro> Using the local AWS Emulator (the environment variables
      are already set in this shell), create a DynamoDB table
      "kiro-demo" with a string key "id", put an item
      {id: "item-1", msg: "hello from kiro"}, then read it
      back with get-item.

$ aws dynamodb create-table --table-name kiro-demo \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST

$ aws dynamodb put-item --table-name kiro-demo \
    --item '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}, "msg": {"S": "hello from kiro"}}'

$ aws dynamodb get-item --table-name kiro-demo --key '{"id": {"S": "item-1"}}' To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual. Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java . For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust . You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process. use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions};
use aws_sdk_dynamodb::types::{
    AttributeDefinition, AttributeValue, BillingMode, KeySchemaElement, KeyType,
    ScalarAttributeType,
};

#[tokio::test]
async fn put_then_get_returns_the_item() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default());
    let config = aws_config::defaults(aws_config::BehaviorVersion::latest())
        .http_client(emulator.http_client())
        .region(aws_config::Region::new("us-east-1"))
        .credentials_provider(emulator.aws_credentials_provider())
        .load()
        .await;
    let ddb = aws_sdk_dynamodb::Client::new(&config);

    ddb.create_table()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .attribute_definitions(
            AttributeDefinition::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").attribute_type(ScalarAttributeType::S)
                .build().unwrap())
        .key_schema(
            KeySchemaElement::builder()
                .attribute_name("id").key_type(KeyType::Hash)
                .build().unwrap())
        .billing_mode(BillingMode::PayPerRequest)
        .send().await.unwrap();

    ddb.put_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .item("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .item("msg", AttributeValue::S("hi".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();

    let got = ddb.get_item()
        .table_name("emulator-demo-table")
        .key("id", AttributeValue::S("item-1".into()))
        .send().await.unwrap();
    assert_eq!(got.item().unwrap().get("msg").unwrap().as_s().unwrap(), "hi");
} When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off. How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates. With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better. If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub. How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline , and AWS CodeCommit , so it stays current with AWS as those models change. One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository. How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships. Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production. Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation. If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation. Updated on November 12, 2026: Added links to the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

title: Albany Man Sentenced to 120 Months for Receiving Child Pornography
body: Press Release Albany Man Sentenced to 120 Months for Receiving Child Pornography Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release U.S. Attorney's Office,               Northern District of New York USANYN-MediaInquiry@usa.doj.gov On November 10, 2026, Gregory Conrad Puzio, a/k/a “Tony G.,” age 41, of Albany, New York, was sentenced to 120 months’ imprisonment for receiving child pornography.  First Assistant United States Attorney John A. Sarcone III; Anthony Patrone, Special Agent in Charge of the Buffalo Field Office of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI); and New York State Police (NYSP) Superintendent Steven G. James made the announcement. As part of his previously entered guilty plea, Puzio admitted that in February 2025, he used a messaging application to receive child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including a video where a child victim was sexually abused and beaten.  In late June 2025, Puzio was charged by local authorities with use of a child in a sexual performance and possessing a sexual performance by a child based on this conduct but was subsequently released on bond.  After a federal complaint was filed on July 8, 2025, federal agents arrested Puzio and he did not contest federal detention. First Assistant United States Attorney Sarcone stated: “Puzio traded in grotesque videos of children being sexually abused and viciously beaten.  After he was released by a New York State court, my office and our partners took immediate action to make sure that this child predator would not be back in the community to engage in further crimes against the most vulnerable among us. This administration shall continue to act swiftly to protect the citizens of the Northern District of New York when the state, with its failed policies when it comes to protecting its citizens from dangerous criminals such as Puzio, allows them to come back into the community pending adjudication.” HSI Special Agent in Charge Patrone stated: “The abuse depicted in the material Gregory Puzio received is profoundly disturbing, and children deserve to be protected from those who perpetuate this exploitation. This 120-month sentence reflects the serious consequences for such conduct and the resolve of HSI and our partners to identify offenders, support victims, and safeguard children. I thank HSI Albany, the New York State Police, the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General, and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for their determined work on this investigation and prosecution.” New York State Police Superintendent Steven G. James said, “Behind every image of child sexual abuse is a real child who has suffered unimaginable harm. This sentence holds Gregory Puzio accountable for his role in perpetuating that abuse. I commend our investigators and federal partners for their work on this case and their continued commitment to protecting children and bringing those who exploit them to justice.” U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino also imposed a 15-year term of supervised release to follow Puzio’s release from prison.  As part of his plea agreement, Puzio agreed to forfeit the phone he used to receive child pornography. This case was investigated by HSI and the NYSP, with assistance from the United States Postal Service’s Office of Inspector General.  Assistant U.S. Attorney Joshua R. Rosenthal prosecuted this case as part of Project Safe Childhood. Project Safe Childhood is a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse. Led by the U.S. Attorneys' Offices and the Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS), Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state and local resources to better locate, apprehend and prosecute individuals who exploit children via the Internet, as well as to identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc . Updated November 11, 2026 Topic Project Safe Childhood Component USAO - New York, Northern
